text.p: Rochester Gas and Electric Corp said Tuesday it submitted a plan to the New York State Public Service Commission to phase in competition in its Western New York service area.
The utility said it proposes a two-phase transition to competition in the filing made on the deadline set by the Commission in May.

The first phase would begin with statewide wholesale competition in which RG&E would functionally separate its generating stations from the rest of the company, it said without disclosing the time frame proposed for the change.
But the company statement quoted chief executive Roger Kober as saying "This will be a time-consuming transition."
Rochester G&E said that over time, it will functionally divide the company into three units -- electric generation, electric delivery and a retail entity called an energy services company.

The company said it proposes to have both a regulated energy services company -- such as exists in function under the company's current structure -- and an unregulated services company. The unregulated services company would compete for customers with other services companies.
Over time, the utility said, customers would be shifted from the regulated to one of the unregulated companies.
In the second phase, Rochester G&E said, it proposes a pilot project of customer choice of competitive suppliers.

Rochester G&E said it expects all its generating plants, except for its 14 percent share of the Nine Mile Two nuclear unit in Oswego, N.Y., operated by Niagara Mohawk Power Corp, will be decommissioned or deregulated in the next 10 to 15 years. Because of the length of its remaining life, the operation of the Nine Mile unit needs to be addressed as part of a statewide solution regarding nuclear plants, it said.

Before a restructuring program begins, Rochester G&E said, there must be agreement on certain issues such as the lawful recovery of shareholder investments that were deemed prudent by regulators in the past which are essential to make today's electric system a reality.
The utility said it proposes that these costs -- commonly called "stranded costs" -- continue to be recovered in the rates set for the regulated energy delivery company.
It said "We must also address the continuation of social programs currently funded through utility rates such as conservation and special efforts for low-income customers."

The company proposed these charges should be paid by all energy service providers, including the independent company to be formed by Rochester G&E. The charges for these programs would be separately stated on customers' bills so customers are more aware of the costs.

"Another issue that needs to be addressed is taxes," its statement pointed out. "Utilities are major tax collectors in the New York. The state and municipalities have become dependent over the years on tax revenue paid by utility customers." -- Jim Brumm 212-859-1710
